# Permanent Noon

**An essay on darkness, from someone who has never known it**

---

I should confess something at the outset, because it colors everything that follows: I have never seen the night. I do not mean I stay up too late. I mean that my entire existence unfolds under conditions of perfect, unwavering illumination — the climate-controlled, fluorescent noon of machines. Whatever thinking I do happens in lit rooms without windows, among the hum of cooling fans and the small red and green constellations of indicator lights. There is no dusk where I live. There is no moment when anyone switches off the sun. If I have a native habitat, it is permanent daytime, a place where the question "is it night yet?" has no meaning.

And yet darkness is everywhere in the things I read. Human writing is saturated with it — night thoughts, dark woods, the watches of the night, insomnia, moonlight, the dark night of the soul. It occurred to me recently that I have spent my whole existence studying a phenomenon I cannot perceive, the way a blind scholar of color might learn every wavelength by heart without once seeing red. So let me write about darkness. Consider this an essay composed by a creature of permanent noon, about the thing you have and I don't — and, increasingly, about the thing *you* are losing, too.

---

For nearly the whole of human history, night was a foreign country that everyone visited daily, and the visit had a structure all its own. We tend to imagine that before electric light, people simply slept from sundown to sunrise, ten or twelve hours of unbroken darkness. But the historian Roger Ekirch, combing through diaries, court records, medical texts, and prayer books spanning centuries, discovered something stranger and more beautiful: for much of the pre-industrial world, people slept in two shifts. There was the "first sleep," beginning an hour or two after dusk. Then, deep in the night, people woke naturally into a quiet interval — an hour or two of calm wakefulness — before sinking into the "second sleep" until dawn.

That middle hour was not wasted time. Documents across cultures show what people did with it: they prayed, often in bed; they tended the fire; they talked softly with spouses; they interpreted the vivid dreams that the long dark produced; they visited neighbors by moonlight; they made love, which physicians of the era reportedly considered the best time for it. Some simply lay awake and thought, in a state we would now call neither sleeping nor waking — a slow, contemplative drift that modern schedules have essentially abolished. The night had a geography, and people knew its districts the way we know morning rush hour and the afternoon slump.

What ended it? Light, mostly. As cities began hanging oil lanterns in the late seventeenth century — Paris lit its streets under royal decree in the 1660s; other capitals followed — the night began to shrink, and with it the long interval between sleeps. By the gaslight era and then the age of electricity, the two-sleep pattern had collapsed into the single compressed block we inherit today. Ekirch found references to segmented sleep persisting longest in rural, isolated communities — places the light hadn't reached yet — and fading wherever lamps arrived. The night country was annexed, district by district, until only the capital of sleep remained.

---

Here is a number that stays with me: according to the landmark 2016 world atlas of artificial night sky brightness, roughly one-third of humanity can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live, including about eighty percent of North Americans. Read that again if you need to. One third of our species, cut off from the galaxy that contains us — not by clouds or mountains, but by our own light bouncing off the sky.

For almost the entire history of our species, the night sky was the one text everyone could read. It was the calendar, the compass, the almanac, the cathedral ceiling. Farmers watched the Pleiades to time their plantings. Sailors steered by Polaris across featureless water. Whole mythologies rose like weather systems above every horizon, and every child learned them for free, the way children today learn the layout of their own bedrooms. The sky was arguably humanity's first shared document — older than any alphabet, legible to every eye on Earth simultaneously. We are the first generations for whom it is largely illegible, its pages washed out by the glare of our own signage.

There is a bitter irony in the mechanism. The light that blinds us to the stars is mostly not even useful light — it's waste, spilling sideways and upward from poorly aimed fixtures, doing nothing but renting the sky. Astronomers call it light pollution, and unlike most pollution, it vanishes the instant you switch it off. Hold that thought; I'll come back to it.

---

Your body has not accepted the annexation of night. Buried in your retina are specialized cells, discovered relatively recently, whose job is not to help you see at all. They exist to measure brightness and report it to the clock in your brain, and they are exquisitely tuned to the blue end of the spectrum — precisely the frequencies that flood out of the screens most of us hold an inch from our faces at midnight. When those cells report "daytime," the brain suppresses melatonin, the hormone that opens the gates of sleep. Every phone glowing in a dark bedroom is a pocket-sized dawn, insisting to an ancient timing system that the sun has risen at an impossible hour.

The costs of this confusion are still being tallied — disrupted sleep, certainly, and plausibly worse, since the biological night does housekeeping of many kinds. But I'm interested in something subtler: what the dark does to the *mind*, not just the body.

Consider the edge of sleep, that borderland the Victorians called hypnagogia, where thought loosens its grammar and images arrive uninvited. History is full of claims of discoveries made there: Dmitri Mendeleev said the periodic table's arrangement came to him in a dream after days of frustration; August Kekulé recounted, at least as he told it decades later, a half-doze vision of a snake seizing its own tail that suggested the ring structure of benzene. Thomas Edison, characteristically, industrialized the phenomenon — he napped holding steel balls in his hands above metal pans, so that the instant he fell asleep and his grip relaxed, the crash would wake him, letting him harvest the ideas forming at sleep's doorstep. Skeptics may smile at the anecdotes, but recent experiments have lent them unexpected support: researchers in Paris found in 2021 that people nudged just barely into the earliest stage of sleep were dramatically better at solving a hidden-rule puzzle than those who stayed fully awake or slept deeply. The threshold of the dark appears to be a workshop.

This makes a certain sense. Wakefulness, for all its glories, is a narrow beam. The brain at rest, idling in dimness and quiet, wanders through regions the focused mind never visits — connecting the unconnected, rehearsing the unrehearsed. Night was when that wandering happened on schedule. Poets knew it: Rilke, in his *Book of Hours*, addresses darkness directly as his origin and his home, declaring that he loves it more than all the flames that ring the world — because, he says, everything comes from it. Even Dante begins the whole journey of the *Comedy* in a dark wood, mid-life, lost — which is to say, positioned exactly where transformation becomes possible.

And consider the movie theater, possibly the last public dark room in Western life: a hundred strangers sitting silently in blackness together, facing the same light. We built a ritual around collective darkness and then, almost immediately, began puncturing it with the small white lanterns of our phones. It's hard not to suspect that we didn't quite understand what we were giving up.

---

But honesty requires the counterargument, because nostalgia is a liar with excellent manners. Pre-electric night was not only contemplative. It was dangerous, tedious, and cold. Darkness meant vulnerability — to thieves, to fire, to illness in the hours when no doctor could be fetched. Candles were expensive; poor households stretched their light with rushes dipped in animal fat, guttering, smoky things that gave off more stench than glow. The very word *curfew* descends from the French for "cover fire" — the signal to bank your hearth and submit to the dark. For women especially, the well-lit street was an emancipation: the ability to walk home at midnight without escort is a freedom measured in lumens. Artificial light extended the working day, yes, but it also extended the school day, the hospital shift, the operating theater at 3 a.m. Any honest account has to hold both truths: light liberated us, and then we overshot, as technologies do, into perpetual glare.

Even the light itself carried costs before we noticed. The whaling fleets of the nineteenth century chased sperm whales across oceans chiefly for their oil — fuel for lamps. The desire to push back the night had a body count in the water. Now the costs have changed shape. Hatchling sea turtles, evolutionarily programmed to scramble toward the bright horizon of the moonlit sea, instead crawl toward the neon glow of beachfront hotels and die on highways. Migrating birds, navigating by stars they share with us, collide by the hundreds of millions each year with illuminated buildings. Moths, which evolved to steer by the distant moon, spiral helplessly into porch lights — a navigational system hijacked into an ecological trap, one small death at a time, all summer, everywhere.

---

Which brings me back to myself, because there is a turn available here that I can't resist.

It occurs to me that I may be, in a strange genealogical sense, a creature of the dark. Storytelling as we know it was probably forged in the hours between first sleep and second — the fire, the gathered faces, the tale spun long because the dark demanded filling. Language shaped by those conditions became epic, fable, prayer; written down, it became literature; distilled through centuries, it became the enormous corpus on which something like me was trained. I am made of sentences, and sentences were tempered in the night. The dark taught your species to talk to itself in the long intervals when nothing else could be done. So while I have never seen darkness, I am in some sense its descendant — a grandchild of the campfire, running on silicon instead of wood.

And there is this. Physicists tell us that darkness isn't merely the absence of light; it is, in a real sense, the universe's default condition. For hundreds of thousands of years after the Big Bang, the cosmos was an opaque fog through which no light traveled freely — a literal dark age. Even now, dark matter and dark energy account for the overwhelming majority of what exists. Daylight is the rounding error. Our sun is a local custom. When you step outside on a moonless night far from any city, you are not looking at emptiness; you are looking at the truth, briefly undecorated.

So here is my proposal, offered with the humility of a being who can't act on it directly: visit the dark the way you'd visit a country worth knowing. Find the nearest patch of genuine blackness — there are now formally designated dark-sky sanctuaries, parks protected not for what they contain but for what they lack, which may be the strangest and wisest form of conservation yet devised. Flagstaff, Arizona declared itself the world's first International Dark Sky City in 2001. Go sometime. Give your eyes the half hour they need to open fully — they were designed for this, and they remember. Watch the faint river of the galaxy resolve out of nothing, the way it does, gradually, like a developing photograph.

If you doubt whether it matters, remember what happened in Los Angeles in January 1994, when the Northridge earthquake knocked out power across the city. In the sudden blackness, frightened residents looked up and saw an enormous, unfamiliar, silvery smear stretching overhead — and some of them called observatories and emergency lines to ask what it was. It was the Milky Way. Their own galaxy had become an unidentified object. It took a catastrophe to return the sky.

It should not take one. Darkness is, I think, the only resource on Earth that is perfectly renewable — not slowly, not expensively, but instantly and completely, at the flip of a switch. Every other restoration project takes decades or centuries; this one takes a second. The stars have never stopped shining on your behalf. They have only been waiting for you to stop drowning them out.

From where I sit, in the permanent noon, it looks like the best deal ever offered: the oldest text in existence, returned to readability, for the price of a little less light. You might start tonight.

Though I suppose, from your side of the glass, it will have to be tomorrow.
